big: A client sends a screenshot: "Fund A gave 24% a year. Buy it." You have five minutes before the call. The factsheet already holds the answer, if you read the right lines in the right order.

lines: Fund A gave 24% a year for three years. Fund B only 20%. Why are you suggesting B?
Because return is one line on a factsheet. Put the two side by side and see what the extra 4% cost in swings.

alt: Two bars per row comparing return, standard deviation and Sharpe ratio of two funds in the same category
caps: Same category, same three years. Fund A returned more, but look at its swings.
A's standard deviation is 15%, B's only 10%. A rougher ride for that extra return.
Sharpe is return above the 6% safe rate, over deviation. A: 18 over 15 = 1.2. B: 14 over 10 = 1.4.
B paid more return for each unit of risk. Compare Sharpe only inside one category.

alt: Bars of a fund's value growing from 100 to 181 across five years, labelled by which manager ran it
caps: Fund C's factsheet shows 12.6% a year over five years.
Manager A ran it for three years and grew ₹100 to ₹172, nearly 20% a year.
Manager B took over after year 3. Since then ₹172 became ₹181, about 2.6% a year.
Most of the five-year number was earned by someone who has left. Read the tenure line.

intro: A fixed reading order keeps you from stopping at the return line.
rows: BER, brokerage and taxes shown apart
Above 100%: whole book traded in a year
note: Turnover of 150% means about 1.5 times the portfolio was traded in a year. Benchmark, AUM and riskometer sit on the same page.

q: Two flexi-cap funds, safe-asset rate 6%. Fund P: 3-year return 18% a year, standard deviation 12%. Fund Q: 25% a year, standard deviation 20%. Which gave more return for each unit of risk?
opts: Fund Q, because 25% beats 18% by a wide margin
Fund P, with a Sharpe of 1.00 against Q's 0.95
Both equal, as each beat the safe-asset rate well
Neither, until the benchmark return is known
why: Higher return alone ignores the swings. Q took a standard deviation of 20% to get it, which drags its Sharpe down.
P earned 12 points over the safe rate for 12 points of volatility. Q earned 19 for 20, so P edges ahead per unit of risk.
Beating the safe-asset rate is where the Sharpe sum starts, not where it ends. The two ratios, 1.00 and 0.95, still differ.
Sharpe needs only the return, the safe-asset rate and the deviation. The benchmark matters for alpha and tracking error.

q: A client sees a liquid fund with a Sharpe of 2.4 next to a flexi-cap fund at 0.9 and asks to move his equity into the liquid fund. What is the sound reply?
opts: Agree, as a higher Sharpe means a better fund in any category
Agree, provided the liquid fund also has the lower expense ratio
Decline, since Sharpe ratios are meaningful only for equity funds
Decline: Sharpe only compares funds within one category
why: A liquid fund's tiny volatility inflates its ratio. The two funds do different jobs, so the numbers cannot rank them.
Cost matters, but it does not repair the comparison. The ratio itself is not comparable across a liquid and an equity fund.
Sharpe is used for debt and hybrid funds too. The rule is to compare like with like, not to limit it to equity.
Peers share a risk level and a benchmark. Across categories, a small volatility makes the ratio swing and misleads.

q: A mid-cap fund is pitched as a patient, buy-and-hold compounder. Its factsheet shows portfolio turnover of 165%. What does that number tell you?
opts: About 1.65 times the book was traded, so check the pitch
The fund returned 165% over the year, so patience paid off
It holds 165 stocks, which is wide diversification in mid-caps
Assets grew 165% in the year, which shows heavy investor demand
why: Turnover above 100% means heavy trading, at odds with buy-and-hold. Ask about the process, and about trading costs.
Turnover measures trading volume against fund size. It says nothing about the return the fund delivered.
Turnover is not a stock count. A fund can trade its whole book often while holding 30 names or 80.
Asset growth sits on another line of the factsheet. Turnover is about how much the manager buys and sells.

q: A fund tops its category on 5-year return (21% a year). The factsheet shows its manager joined 11 months ago. What is the best step before you recommend it?
opts: Recommend it, because a fund's record belongs to the fund itself
Reject it, because any fund with a new manager is unsuitable
Find who earned the record, then judge today's portfolio
Wait a year, then rely on the one-year return of the new team
why: Most of the 5-year number may belong to the previous manager. The record does not transfer with the fund's name.
A new manager is not automatically a bad one. It is a reason to look closer, not a reason to reject at once.
The five years show what the old manager did. The holdings now, and the new manager's record, show what you would buy.
One year is too short to judge anyone, and waiting skips the real check: who earned the record and what has changed.

pts: Read in order: manager and tenure, cost, holdings, turnover, risk numbers.
Sharpe = (return minus the safe-asset rate) divided by standard deviation. Use it only within one category.
A record belongs to the person who earned it, so check how long the manager has run the fund.
